title: Biomimicry Principles in Architecture for Promoting Healthy Buildings: An Analysis of Relevant Literatures
research_focus: To systematically review and analyze existing literature on biomimicry principles in architecture for promoting healthy buildings, identify current knowledge gaps, and determine future research directions.

sample_context.description: Literature on biomimicry architecture, healthy buildings, and healthy building criteria, sourced from MDPI, ScienceDirect, Scopus, ResearchGate, Taylor & Francis, and JARS databases, published between 2000-2024.
sample_context.setting: Academic databases and scientific publications related to architecture, sustainability, and health.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry principles in architectural design (e.g., resource efficiency, evolution for survival, adapting to changing conditions, local attunement, life-friendly chemistry, Nature as Model, Measure, Mentor)
findings.consequent: Promotion of healthy buildings and sustainable architectural design, enhanced human health and well-being (physical, mental, social), energy conservation, and environmental sustainability.
findings.description: Nature-inspired design strategies, drawing from natural forms, processes, and ecosystems, are integrated into architectural design to create structures that are environmentally friendly, efficient, resilient, and conducive to human health and well-being.

findings.antecedent: Implementation of healthy building criteria (e.g., good air conditioning, material health control, lighting and views, noise control, good building plan, water quality, environmental sustainability)
findings.consequent: Enhanced occupant well-being (physical, psychological, social health), improved indoor air quality, thermal comfort, reduced stress, better sleep quality, and energy conservation.
findings.description: Key metrics and design considerations, often aligned with WELL Building Standard concepts, are crucial for creating built environments that positively impact occupant health and well-being across physical, psychological, and social dimensions.

findings.antecedent: Challenges in biomimicry implementation (e.g., lack of knowledge, high initial cost, scalability issues for larger buildings/urban areas, need for interdisciplinary collaboration, regulatory barriers, localized solutions)
findings.consequent: Limited adoption and realization of the full potential for healthy, sustainable buildings, and increased difficulty in translating nature-based strategies across diverse geographical areas.
findings.description: Various barriers, including economic, educational, technological, and regulatory factors, hinder the widespread and effective integration of biomimicry principles in architectural design and construction.

findings.antecedent: Application of biomimicry in building design (e.g., natural cooling/heating systems inspired by termite mounds, self-cleaning surfaces imitating lotus leaves, efficient material use, durable structures, enhanced indoor air quality, natural light, circadian rhythm regulation)
findings.consequent: Reduced operating costs, increased building durability and resilience, improved occupant health and productivity, higher property values, and significant contributions to environmental sustainability (e.g., resource conservation, waste reduction, pollution mitigation).
findings.description: Multifaceted advantages of integrating nature-inspired designs in architecture, leading to economic, environmental, and human health benefits, as demonstrated by case studies like the Bullitt Center, Bangkok Tree House, EDITT Tower, and Pearl River Tower.

themes_or_constructs: Biomimicry in Architecture to support human health and the environment
Biomimicry in Architecture close to Healthy Environment
mechanism_candidates: Mimicking natural patterns and systems fosters physical and mental health benefits by prioritizing natural light, plant life, and green spaces.
Biomimetic designs regulate circadian rhythms, enhancing sleep quality and general health.
Natural cooling and heating strategies (e.g., inspired by termite mounds) reduce reliance on mechanical systems and lower energy consumption.
Self-cleaning surfaces (e.g., inspired by lotus leaves) reduce maintenance needs.
Efficient material use, inspired by natural systems, reduces construction waste and costs.
Durable and resilient structures, mimicking natural systems, require fewer repairs and extend building lifecycles.
Enhanced indoor air quality and natural light improve occupant health and productivity.
transferability_limits: Biomimetic solutions are often localized based on specific climates and contexts, making translation to different geographical areas challenging due to varying climatic conditions.
limitations: Lack of knowledge and research on complex inter-relationships between built environment factors and human health.
Architecture profession not mandated to learn about human health in educational curriculum.
Financial limitations often make healthy design features seem 'too expensive or costly'.
Complexity of translating biological concepts into architectural designs.
Lack of proper education and wide understanding of biomimicry principles among architects.
Failure of building codes and regulations to accommodate innovative biomimetic features.
Cost implications due to advanced materials and technology in biomimicry innovations.

paper_metadata.title: BIOMORPHIC ARCHITECTURE APPROACH IN BUILDING FORM BASED ON ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERN
paper_metadata.crossref_title: BIOMORPHIC ARCHITECTURE APPROACH IN BUILDING FORM BASED ON ENVIRONMENTAL CONCERN
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Nature is an excellent learning resource for humans, especially for nature as a source of inspiration in the architectural design. Biomorphic is one of the themes in the architectural approach that has a principle concern for the environment (nature), in which this approach was born from the idea of the importance of nature and oriented to the environment, including climate. The shape, material, structure and mechanisms in the universe, can be used as the basic idea formed in the design of architecture through a process of collaboration between humans and nature itself. The method used in this study is a qualitative design method, through analysis approach biomorphic design theme Architecture. Sea World is the main object in the design, which is a vehicle for recreational and educative to showcase marine life and its beauty in a large aquarium. Sea World that use biomorphic theme, designed by using the analogy of a stingray wing motion transformation into shape, hoping to bring the dynamic character of Sea World and attract visitors as well as having the characteristics of the natural inspiration.
